name: Achish (king of the Philistines)
title: Philistine king of Gath
summary: Achish, son of Maacah, was a Philistine king over the city of Gath – one of the five major Philistine city-states. He plays a prominent role in the accounts about David, who twice sought refuge with him while fleeing from King Saul. During the first visit, David was recognized by Achish's servants as an Israelite warrior hero, and David saved himself by pretending to be insane, which caused Achish to send him away. On the second visit, David came with 600 men and their families, and Achish gave them the city of Ziklag to live in. However, David deceived Achish by attacking the Geshurites, Girzites, and Amalekites, while telling the king that he had raided the southern regions of Judah. Achish came to trust David so much that he wanted him as his personal bodyguard in the war against Israel, but the other Philistine rulers opposed this. In 1 Kings 2:39 an Achish, son of Maacah, is mentioned as king of Gath during Solomon's reign – it is debated whether this is the same person or a descendant. In the heading of Psalm 34 he is referred to by the Philistine royal title Abimelech.

keyEvents.title: David's first flight to Achish
keyEvents.description: David fled to Achish in Gath to escape Saul, but became afraid when Achish's servants recognized him as Israel's warrior hero. David pretended to be insane, and Achish sent him away, criticizing his servants for bringing a 'madman' to him.

keyEvents.title: David seeks permanent refuge with Achish
keyEvents.description: David returned to Achish with 600 men and their families. This time, Achish welcomed him and gave him the town of Ziklag to live in. When Saul heard that David was with Achish, he stopped looking for him.

keyEvents.title: David deceives Achish
keyEvents.description: David carried out raids against the Geshurites, Girzites, and Amalekites, but told Achish that he had attacked the southern regions of Judah. Achish fully trusted David and believed he had made himself hated among his own people.

keyEvents.title: Achish wants David to join the war against Israel
keyEvents.description: Achish appointed David as his bodyguard and wanted to take him with him in the war against Israel. However, the other Philistine rulers refused to accept David's participation, and Achish had to send David back to Ziklag with a heavy heart.

keyEvents.title: Achish mentioned during Solomon's reign
keyEvents.description: An Achish, son of Maacah, was king of Gath when two of Shimei's slaves fled there. Shimei went to Gath to retrieve them and thus broke his oath to Solomon. It is debated whether this Achish is the same person as Achish son of Maoch, or if it concerns a descendant.

versions.summary: Achish was king over the Philistine city of Gath. He is best known for having given David refuge twice when David fled from King Saul, showing surprising hospitality toward Israel's future king.
versions.title: The hospitable king of the Philistines
versions.reason: [minor] The title 'The Philistine King's Hospitality' is somewhat nuanced. Achish was specifically king of Gath, not over all the Philistines. Additionally, 'hospitality' is an interpretation that does not fully cover his role – he was also deceived by David. A more precise title would have been 'Philistine King of Gath'.; [minor] The summary is acceptable but could be expanded slightly to mention that David deceived Achish, which is a central part of the story. It should also be noted that Achish is referenced in the heading of Psalm 34 (where he is called Abimelech), providing important context.; [minor] Achish was not merely 'king', but specifically one of the Philistine city-kings (seren/prince). The role 'Philistine prince' or 'city-king' could be considered as an addition for greater precision.; [minor] The reference in 1 Sam 21 starts from verse 10 in many traditions, but in the Hebrew Bible this passage begins at 21:11. Verse divisions may vary. The current layout (21:10-15) aligns with common Norwegian numbering and is acceptable.; [minor] This event ('Achish sends David away') overlaps strongly with the first event and partly uses the same verses (21:14-15). It could be considered to merge these into one event to avoid duplication.; [major] Achish's father is named Maok according to 1 Sam 27:2. The value 'maok' is correct as an identifier. However, 1 Kings 2:39 mentions an Achish, son of Ma'aka, as king in Gath. There is debate over whether this is the same person or a descendant. This should be reflected in a footnote.; [minor] The lifespan 'c. 1020-980 BC' is somewhat narrow. If the Achish in 1 Kings 2:39 is the same person, he was also active around the 960s BC (during Solomon's reign). A broader dating such as 'c. 1020-960 BC' or a note about the uncertainty should be considered.

versions.summary: Achish was a Philistine king over the city of Gath and son of Maok. He is known from David's time, when David twice sought refuge with him to escape King Saul. During David's first visit, David pretended to be insane, and Achish sent him away. On the second visit, Achish welcomed David and his 600 men and gave them the city of Ziklag to live in. However, David deceived Achish by attacking other peoples while claiming he was raiding Judah. Achish trusted David and wanted him as a bodyguard in the war against Israel, but the other Philistine rulers opposed this. Achish may also be the king of Gath mentioned during Solomon's reign. In the heading to Psalm 34, he is referred to by the Philistine royal title Abimelech.
versions.title: Philistine king of Gath
versions.reason: [minor] Achish was specifically a 'seren' (Philistine city-state ruler), not just a general 'Philistine prince'. The term 'ruler' or 'city king' could be added to reflect his position as leader of one of the five Philistine city-states.; [minor] The phrasing 'while he claimed to raid against Judah' is slightly imprecise. The text in 1 Sam 27:10 states that David claimed to have attacked the southern areas of Judah (the Negev), not that he 'raided against Judah'. A more precise formulation would be 'while he told Achish that he was attacking Judah's southern regions'.; [minor] The last keyEvent about Achish during Solomon's time refers to his father's name as Ma'aka, while the family field uses 'maok'. Both name forms are legitimate variants, but it should be made clearer that these may possibly be two different people.; [minor] The sentence 'Achish may also be the king of Gath mentioned during Solomon's reign' could usefully be clarified by noting that this is Achish son of Ma'aka in 1 Kings 2:39, and that the identification is uncertain due to the long time period between the events.

footnotes.text: The name Achish (Hebrew: אָכִישׁ, 'Akhish') has been linked to the non-Semitic name 'Ikausu' found in Assyrian inscriptions from Ekron (Tel Miqne), which may confirm the Aegean origin of the Philistines. The name may have Indo-European roots.

In the heading of Psalm 34, Achish is called 'Abimelech' (אֲבִימֶלֶךְ). This may be a dynastic title for Philistine kings (cf. Gen 20; 26), similar to 'Pharaoh' for Egyptian kings. The rabbinic tradition explains this by stating that Abimelech was an honorific title used by Philistine rulers.

Archaeological excavations at Tell es-Safi (identified as the biblical Gath) have revealed a large Philistine city with significant Iron Age settlement, confirming Gath's status as an important Philistine city-state during Achish's time.

In 1 Kings 2:39, an Achish, son of Maacah, is mentioned as king of Gath during Solomon's reign. It is debated whether this is the same person as Achish, son of Maoch, in 1 Sam 27:2. The names Maoch and Maacah may be variants of the same name, which supports identifying them as the same person, but the long time period leads some scholars to believe they are father and son.

The Philistine city-states (Gaza, Ashdod, Ashkelon, Ekron, and Gath) were ruled by 'seranim' (סְרָנִים), a term possibly related to the Greek 'tyrannos'. Achish was such a seren, and the other Philistine rulers had authority to override his decisions, as when they refused to let David participate in the war against Israel (1 Sam 29).

Ziklag, the city that Achish granted to David, has been attempted to be identified with several archaeological sites, including Tell esh-Sharia and Khirbet Zayit. More recent excavations at Khirbet al-Ra'i south of Gath have been proposed as a possible candidate, with findings fitting a city in the border area between Philistine and Judahite territory.
